## The plane

The object your program creates and calls every frame.

### Plane

```py
pgp.Plane(
    rect: object | None = None,
    *,
    x_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    y_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    log_x: bool = False,
    log_y: bool = False,
    center: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    scale: float | tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    equal_aspect: bool | None = None,
    theme: GridTheme | None = None,
    interactive: bool = True,
    interaction: InteractionConfig | None = None,
    limits: ViewLimits | None = None,
    renderer: PygameRenderer | None = None,
    sampling: SamplingConfig | None = None,
    cache: bool = True,
)
```

An interactive Cartesian plane drawn into a rectangle of a pygame surface.

The initial view can be given like a graphing calculator's window settings, `x_range=(x_min, x_max)` and `y_range=(y_min, y_max)`, or as a `center` and `scale`. Either axis can be logarithmic.

*Parameters:*

- `rect`: The screen rectangle to draw into. `None` (the default) fills whatever surface `draw_grid` is given and follows it when the window is resized.
- `x_range`: `(x_min, x_max)` to show across the plane's width at first. Overrides `center` and `scale` for the x axis.
- `y_range`: `(y_min, y_max)` to show across the plane's height at first. Overrides `center` and `scale` for the y axis.
- `log_x`: Make the x axis logarithmic (base 10). Only positive x values can be shown.
- `log_y`: Make the y axis logarithmic (base 10). Only positive y values can be shown.
- `center`: World point initially shown at the middle of the plane. Defaults to 0 on a linear axis and 1 on a log axis.
- `scale`: Initial pixels per world unit (per decade on a log axis): one number, or an `(x, y)` pair when the aspect is not equal. Defaults to 50 per unit and 150 per decade.
- `equal_aspect`: Keep both axes at the same scale, so circles stay round. `None` (the default) decides automatically: on, unless both ranges are given (each then fills its axis exactly) or only one axis is logarithmic.
- `theme`: Grid appearance. Defaults to `LIGHT`.
- `interactive`: Whether the built-in pan/zoom controls are active.
- `interaction`: Settings for the built-in controls.
- `limits`: Zoom and pan limits (see `ViewLimits`).
- `renderer`: Renderer to draw with. Planes can share one renderer, and with it their font and label caches.
- `sampling`: How functions are sampled by `plot` (the defaults suit almost every function).
- `cache`: Reuse plots that have not changed since the previous frame (see `cache`). It only saves time; the drawing is the same.

#### Members of `Plane`

- **`plane.view`** (`View`, read only)

  The plane's `View`.

  Use it to read or change the centre, scale and visible bounds directly.

- **`plane.rect`** (`ScreenRect`, read and write)

  The screen rectangle the plane occupies.

  Assign a rectangle (for example a `pygame.Rect`) to move or resize the plane, or `None` to make it fill the surface it is drawn on. Resizing keeps the centre and scale, so more or less of the plane becomes visible.

- **`plane.log_x`** (`bool`, read and write)

  Whether the x axis is logarithmic.

  Assign to switch it: the visible x range is kept where possible (see `View.set_log`) and becomes part of the new home view.

- **`plane.log_y`** (`bool`, read and write)

  Whether the y axis is logarithmic (assign to switch it, as for x).

- **`plane.theme`** (`GridTheme`, read and write)

  The grid's appearance. Assign a new theme to restyle the plane.

- **`plane.sampling`** (`SamplingConfig`, read and write)

  How `plot` samples functions (assign to change it).

- **`plane.cache`** (`bool`, read and write)

  Whether plots that have not changed since the previous frame are reused.

  On by default. A plotting call is reused when it is the same kind of call, in the same place among the frame's calls, with the same view, style and inputs as in the previous frame, and its functions still give exactly the values they gave then (they are checked at every point where they were evaluated). The drawing is then exactly what drawing again would give, so turning the cache off changes only the speed; do so to measure how long drawing takes, or if your functions are not *pointwise* (their value at `x` depends on the other points they are called with).

- **`plane.cache_stats`** (`CacheStats`, read only)

  How many plotting calls were reused (hits) and built again (misses).

- **`plane.clear_cache()`**

  ```py
  plane.clear_cache()
  ```

  Forget every reused plot and grid, and the counts in `cache_stats`.

- **`plane.interaction`** (`InteractionConfig`, read and write)

  Settings of the built-in pan/zoom controls and of dragging points.

- **`plane.renderer`** (`PygameRenderer`, read only)

  The renderer the plane draws with.

- **`plane.last_grid`** (`GridScene | None`, read only)

  The grid drawn by the most recent `draw_grid` call, if any.

  Useful for debugging overlays (it records the chosen spacings).

- **`plane.handle_event()`**

  ```py
  plane.handle_event(event: pygame.event.Event) -> bool
  ```

  Let the plane react to an input event (dragging points, pan, zoom, keys).

  Pass every event, including mouse motion: the plane tracks the cursor to zoom about it and to highlight draggable points under it. A press over a draggable point drags the point; anywhere else it pans.

  *Parameters:*

  - `event`: A pygame event.

  *Returns:* `True` if the plane used the event, so your code can skip handling it again.

- **`plane.update()`**

  ```py
  plane.update() -> bool
  ```

  Advance eased pan/zoom movement, and keep a dragged point under the cursor.

  `draw_grid` calls this automatically, so you only need it if you stop drawing the grid but still want eased movement (and dragging while the view eases) to continue.

  *Returns:* `True` if the view changed.

- **`plane.begin_frame()`**

  ```py
  plane.begin_frame()
  ```

  Start a new frame for the colour palette and the draggable points.

  The next object drawn without a colour gets the first palette colour again, and each draggable point updates its `DraggablePoint.moved` flag. `draw_grid` calls this automatically. Call it yourself only if you draw plots without drawing the grid, so that every object keeps the same palette colour from frame to frame.

- **`plane.draw_grid()`**

  ```py
  plane.draw_grid(surface: pygame.Surface)
  ```

  Draw the background, grid lines, axes and tick labels.

  Drawing is clipped to `rect`, so the plane can share a window with other content. Call it once per frame, before drawing anything that should appear on top of the grid. It also starts a new frame for the colour palette (see `begin_frame`).

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on (usually the display surface).

- **`plane.plot()`**

  ```py
  plane.plot(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      func: Function,
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      domain: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: SamplingConfig | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Plot the graph of an explicit function `y = func(x)`.

  `func` can be vectorised (written with NumPy, the fastest) or work on single numbers only (for example written with `math`). Points where it raises an error or returns NaN or a complex number are left out, and jumps such as the asymptotes of `tan` are not joined up.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `func`: The function to plot.
  - `color`: Line colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Line width in pixels (default 2.5).
  - `opacity`: Line opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `domain`: Only plot where `domain[0] <= x <= domain[1]`.
  - `style`: A reusable `LineStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.
  - `sampling`: Override the plane's sampling settings for this call.

  *Note:* When creating functions in a loop, bind the loop variable as a default argument: `[lambda x, k=k: x**k for k in range(3)]`. Plain `lambda x: x**k` would make every function use the last `k`.

- **`plane.parametric()`**

  ```py
  plane.parametric(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      x: CurveComponent,
      y: CurveComponent,
      t_range: tuple[float, float],
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: CurveSampling | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Plot the parametric curve `(x(t), y(t))` for `t` in `t_range`.

  `x` and `y` are functions of `t`, written like the functions given to `plot` (vectorised or scalar-only, and allowed to fail for some `t`), or plain numbers. The curve is sampled adaptively on screen, so tight turns, loops and spirals stay smooth at any zoom, and jumps and poles are not joined up.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `x`: The x coordinate as a function of `t` (or a number).
  - `y`: The y coordinate as a function of `t` (or a number).
  - `t_range`: `(t_min, t_max)`, for example `(0, 2 * np.pi)`.
  - `color`: Line colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Line width in pixels (default 2.5).
  - `opacity`: Line opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `style`: A reusable `LineStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.
  - `sampling`: How the curve is sampled (see `CurveSampling`; the defaults suit almost every curve).

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If `t_range` is not an increasing pair of numbers.

- **`plane.polar()`**

  ```py
  plane.polar(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      r: CurveComponent,
      theta_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 6.283185307179586),
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: CurveSampling | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Plot the polar curve `r = r(θ)`.

  The point at angle `θ` (radians, anticlockwise from the positive x axis) is `(r cos θ, r sin θ)`; a negative `r` lies on the opposite side of the origin. Angles where `r` is undefined are left out.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `r`: The radius as a function of `θ` (or a number, for a circle).
  - `theta_range`: `(θ_min, θ_max)`. The default is one full turn; spirals and curves such as `r = cos(θ / 3)` need more.
  - `color`: Line colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Line width in pixels (default 2.5).
  - `opacity`: Line opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `style`: A reusable `LineStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.
  - `sampling`: How the curve is sampled (see `CurveSampling`).

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If `theta_range` is not an increasing pair of numbers.

- **`plane.implicit()`**

  ```py
  plane.implicit(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      func: PlaneFunction,
      level: float | Sequence[float] = 0.0,
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: ImplicitSampling | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Plot the implicit curve `func(x, y) = level`.

  The curve is found on a grid of samples a couple of pixels apart (marching squares), refined wherever it crosses the grid, so it can be any shape: closed loops, several separate pieces, branches that cross. Where `func` changes sign without passing through `level` (a pole such as `y - tan(x)`, or a jump such as `y - floor(x)`) no line is drawn, and the curve stops where `func` is undefined.

  `func` must change sign across the curve: a curve where it only touches `level` (`(x - y)**2 = 0`) is not found, so write such equations without the square. Features smaller than about two pixels may be missed.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `func`: `F(x, y)`, taking and returning NumPy arrays (or plain numbers, at some cost in speed). It may raise errors or return NaN where it is undefined.
  - `level`: The value of `func` along the curve, so that `plane.implicit(screen, lambda x, y: x**2 + y**2, 9)` draws the circle `x² + y² = 9`. A sequence of values draws a curve for each, all in one style (contour lines, like the height lines of a map); this is much faster than one call per value, as `func` is evaluated only once.
  - `color`: Line colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Line width in pixels (default 2.5).
  - `opacity`: Line opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `style`: A reusable `LineStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.
  - `sampling`: How the curve is searched for (see `ImplicitSampling`).

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If a level is not a finite number.

- **`plane.points()`**

  ```py
  plane.points(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      points: ArrayLike,
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      radius: float | None = None,
      marker: MarkerShape | None = None,
      edge_color: ColorLike | None = None,
      edge_width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: PointStyle | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Draw points as markers that keep the same size in pixels at every zoom.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `points`: A single point `(x, y)`, a sequence of points, or an `(N, 2)` array. Points with a NaN coordinate are skipped.
  - `color`: Marker colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `radius`: Marker size in pixels (default 4.5).
  - `marker`: `"circle"` (default), `"square"`, `"diamond"`, `"cross"` or `"plus"`.
  - `edge_color`: Colour of an outline around each marker.
  - `edge_width`: Outline thickness in pixels (default 1.5).
  - `opacity`: Opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `style`: A reusable `PointStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.

- **`plane.polyline()`**

  ```py
  plane.polyline(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      points: ArrayLike,
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      closed: bool = False,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Draw straight lines through a sequence of world-space vertices.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `points`: The vertices, in order: a sequence of points or an `(N, 2)` array. A vertex with a NaN coordinate breaks the line.
  - `color`: Line colour (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Line width in pixels (default 2.5).
  - `opacity`: Line opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `closed`: Connect the last vertex back to the first.
  - `style`: A reusable `LineStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.

- **`plane.polygon()`**

  ```py
  plane.polygon(
      surface: pygame.Surface,
      points: ArrayLike,
      *,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      fill: bool | None = None,
      fill_color: ColorLike | None = None,
      fill_opacity: float | None = None,
      fill_rule: FillRule | None = None,
      style: PolygonStyle | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Draw a polygon: a translucent fill with an outline.

  The polygon's vertices are in world units, so it grows and shrinks with the zoom. Its outline width is in pixels.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `points`: The vertices of the ring, in order (it closes itself).
  - `color`: Outline colour, also used for the fill unless `fill_color` is given (default: the next palette colour).
  - `width`: Outline width in pixels (default 2.5; `0` for none).
  - `opacity`: Outline opacity in `[0, 1]`.
  - `fill`: Whether to fill the polygon (default `True`).
  - `fill_color`: Fill colour (default: the outline colour).
  - `fill_opacity`: Fill opacity in `[0, 1]` (default 0.25).
  - `fill_rule`: `"nonzero"` (default) or `"evenodd"`, for polygons whose edges cross.
  - `style`: A reusable `PolygonStyle`. The other keyword arguments override its fields.

- **`plane.draggable()`**

  ```py
  plane.draggable(
      position: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
      *,
      lock: Lock | None = None,
      curve: CurveSpec | None = None,
      t: float | None = None,
      x_range: Range | None = None,
      y_range: Range | None = None,
      color: ColorLike | None = None,
      style: PointStyle | None = None,
      coordinates: Coordinates = 'hover',
      enabled: bool = True,
  ) -> DraggablePoint
  ```

  Create a point that the user can drag with the mouse.

  Create the point once, before the main loop. `handle_event` then drags it, your code reads its `DraggablePoint.x` and `DraggablePoint.y` every frame, and `draw_draggables` draws it:

  ```py
  a = plane.draggable((1, 2))                       # free
  s = plane.draggable((-3, 0.5), lock="x", y_range=(0, 1))  # a slider
  c = plane.draggable(curve=(np.cos, np.sin, (0, 2 * np.pi)))
  ```

  *Parameters:*

  - `position`: Where the point starts (needed for free and locked points). A point on a curve starts at the point of the curve nearest to it, or at `t` if no position is given.
  - `lock`: `"x"` keeps x fixed so the point slides vertically, `"y"` keeps y fixed so it slides horizontally; `None` (the default) lets it move freely.
  - `curve`: `(x, y, t_range)`: keep the point on the parametric curve `(x(t), y(t))`, written as for `parametric`. Dragging follows the curve from where the point is, jumping to another part of the curve only if it is clearly closer to the cursor.
  - `t`: Starting parameter of a point on a curve (default: the start of `t_range`).
  - `x_range`: Keep x within `(low, high)` (free and locked points).
  - `y_range`: Keep y within `(low, high)` (free and locked points).
  - `color`: Fill colour. The default gives each draggable point its own palette colour, in the order the points were created.
  - `style`: A `PointStyle`. The default is a larger marker than plain points, outlined in the background colour.
  - `coordinates`: Show the point's coordinates `"hover"` (while hovered or dragged, the default), `"always"` or `"never"`.
  - `enabled`: Whether the point can be dragged.

  *Returns:* The point, registered with this plane until its `DraggablePoint.remove` is called.

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If the options conflict (`lock` with `curve`, ranges with `curve`), a free or locked point has no position, or a range or position is invalid.

- **`plane.draggables`** (`tuple[DraggablePoint, ...]`, read only)

  The plane's draggable points, in the order they were created.

- **`plane.dragged`** (`DraggablePoint | None`, read only)

  The draggable point being dragged, if any.

- **`plane.draw_draggables()`**

  ```py
  plane.draw_draggables(surface: pygame.Surface, *points: DraggablePoint)
  ```

  Draw draggable points, with their highlight and coordinates.

  Call it after the plots, so the points sit on top of the curves they control. A hovered or dragged point gets a translucent ring, and its coordinates are shown as set by its `DraggablePoint.coordinates`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `surface`: The surface to draw on.
  - `*points`: The points to draw (default: all of this plane's points, in creation order).

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If a point does not belong to this plane.

- **`plane.to_world()`**

  ```py
  plane.to_world(px: Any, py: Any) -> Any
  ```

  Convert screen coordinates (for example the mouse) to world coordinates.

  *Parameters:*

  - `px`: Screen x coordinate(s) in pixels.
  - `py`: Screen y coordinate(s) in pixels.

  *Returns:* The world coordinates `(x, y)`.

- **`plane.to_screen()`**

  ```py
  plane.to_screen(x: Any, y: Any) -> Any
  ```

  Convert world coordinates to continuous screen coordinates.

  *Parameters:*

  - `x`: World x coordinate(s).
  - `y`: World y coordinate(s).

  *Returns:* The screen coordinates `(p_x, p_y)` in pixels.

- **`plane.set_view()`**

  ```py
  plane.set_view(
      x_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
      y_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
  )
  ```

  Fit the view to show the given world ranges.

  With equal aspect on, the tighter range decides the scale and the other axis shows extra space. On a log axis the range must be positive. An automatic plane that has not been drawn yet fits again once it knows its real size (unless the view is changed before).

  *Parameters:*

  - `x_range`: `(x_min, x_max)` to show across the plane's width.
  - `y_range`: `(y_min, y_max)` to show across the plane's height.

  *Raises:*

  - `ValueError`: If a range is empty, reversed, not finite, or not positive on a log axis.

- **`plane.reset_view()`**

  ```py
  plane.reset_view()
  ```

  Return to the home view (initially the view the plane was created with).

- **`plane.set_home()`**

  ```py
  plane.set_home(state: ViewState | None = None)
  ```

  Change the view that `reset_view` (and the Home key) returns to.

  *Parameters:*

  - `state`: The new home view, or `None` to use the current view.

### show

```py
pgp.show(
    *functions: Function | str | Graph,
    size: tuple[int, int] = (960, 640),
    title: str = 'PyGridPlot',
    theme: GridTheme | None = None,
    x_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    y_range: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    log_x: bool = False,
    log_y: bool = False,
    center: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    scale: float | tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    width: float | None = None,
    fps: int = 60,
)
```

Open a window, draw what is given and run until the window is closed.

Each function or line gets the next colour of the theme's palette. The view options are the same as `Plane`'s, for example `show(np.exp, log_y=True)` or `show(np.sin, x_range=(0, 10))`.

*Parameters:*

- `*functions`: What to draw: functions `y = f(x)`, lines of maths as `Graph.add` reads them (`"x^2 + y^2 = 9"`), or whole `Graph` objects (with their draggable points; a graph with a saved view opens at it, unless view options are given).
- `size`: Initial window size in pixels.
- `title`: Window title.
- `theme`: Plane appearance (defaults to `LIGHT`).
- `x_range`: `(x_min, x_max)` to show at first.
- `y_range`: `(y_min, y_max)` to show at first.
- `log_x`: Make the x axis logarithmic.
- `log_y`: Make the y axis logarithmic.
- `center`: World point initially at the middle of the window.
- `scale`: Initial pixels per world unit (per decade on a log axis).
- `width`: Line width in pixels for the functions and lines (default 2.5).
- `fps`: Frame-rate cap.

*Raises:*

- `ExpressionError`: If a line is not valid.

## Derivatives

Derivatives of any order of functions of one variable, exact for functions written with NumPy.

### derivative

```py
pgp.derivative(func: Function, n: int = 1) -> Derivative
```

Return the `n`-th derivative of a function of one variable.

The result is a function of `x` like any other: plot it, call it at a point, or differentiate it again:

```py
df = derivative(np.sin)        # cos
d3f = derivative(f, 3)
plane.plot(screen, df)
slope = df(1.5)
```

The derivative is exact for functions written with NumPy, and computed numerically for others (see `derivatives`).

*Parameters:*

- `func`: The function, taking and returning numbers or NumPy arrays.
- `n`: The order of the derivative (0 returns the function itself, evaluated robustly).

*Returns:* The derivative.

*Raises:*

- `TypeError`: If `func` is not callable.
- `ValueError`: If `n` is not a whole number in `[0, 40]`.

### derivatives

```py
pgp.derivatives(func: Function, x: Any, n: int) -> Any
```

Return a function's value and its derivatives up to order `n`.

Computing them together costs little more than the highest one alone:

```py
value, slope, curvature = derivatives(f, 1.5, 2)
```

*Parameters:*

- `func`: The function.
- `x`: A number, or an array of numbers.
- `n`: The highest order.

*Returns:* For a number, the tuple `(f(x), f'(x), ..., f⁽ⁿ⁾(x))`; for an array, an array of shape `(n + 1, *x.shape)`. NaN where undefined.

*Raises:*

- `TypeError`: If `func` is not callable.
- `ValueError`: If `n` is not a whole number in `[0, 40]`.

## Draggable points

Points the user drags, created with `Plane.draggable`.

### DraggablePoint

```py
pgp.DraggablePoint(
    view: View,
    position: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    *,
    lock: Lock | None = None,
    curve: CurveSpec | None = None,
    t: float | None = None,
    x_range: Range | None = None,
    y_range: Range | None = None,
    style: PointStyle | None = None,
    color: ColorLike | None = None,
    coordinates: Coordinates = 'hover',
    enabled: bool = True,
    on_remove: Callable[[DraggablePoint], None] | None = None,
)
```

A point that can be dragged with the mouse, freely or along a constraint.

Create points with `Plane.draggable` rather than directly: the plane then routes mouse events to them and draws them.

*Parameters:*

- `view`: The view the point lives in (the plane's).
- `position`: The starting position. For a point on a curve, the point starts at the nearest point of the curve (as seen on screen); without it, at `t`.
- `lock`: `"x"` keeps x fixed, `"y"` keeps y fixed, `None` (the default) lets the point move freely.
- `curve`: `(x, y, t_range)`: keep the point on this parametric curve.
- `t`: Starting parameter of a point on a curve (default: the start of `t_range`).
- `x_range`: Bounds for x, for free and locked points.
- `y_range`: Bounds for y, for free and locked points.
- `style`: How the point looks (default `DEFAULT_DRAGGABLE_STYLE`).
- `color`: Fill colour; `None` gives each point a palette colour, in the order the points were created.
- `coordinates`: When to show the coordinates: `"hover"` (while hovered or dragged), `"always"` or `"never"`.
- `enabled`: Whether the point can be dragged.
- `on_remove`: Called by `remove` (the plane forgets the point).

*Raises:*

- `ValueError`: If the settings conflict or are invalid (for example `lock` together with `curve`, or a position outside a log axis).
- `TypeError`: If a curve component is neither callable nor a number.

#### Members of `DraggablePoint`

- **`draggablePoint.x`** (`float`, read only)

  World x (NaN while a point's curve is undefined at its parameter).

- **`draggablePoint.y`** (`float`, read only)

  World y (NaN while a point's curve is undefined at its parameter).

- **`draggablePoint.position`** (`tuple[float, float]`, read and write)

  The world position `(x, y)`.

  Setting it moves the point as near as its constraint allows: a free point goes there (within its bounds), a locked point too (locks restrict only dragging), and a point on a curve goes to the nearest point of the curve as seen on screen.

- **`draggablePoint.t`** (`float | None`, read and write)

  The curve parameter of a point on a curve (`None` for other points).

  Setting it moves the point to that parameter (clamped to the curve's `t_range`).

- **`draggablePoint.lock`** (`Lock | None`, read only)

  `"x"` or `"y"` for a locked point, `None` otherwise.

- **`draggablePoint.x_range`** (`Range | None`, read only)

  Bounds for x, if any.

- **`draggablePoint.y_range`** (`Range | None`, read only)

  Bounds for y, if any.

- **`draggablePoint.curve`** (`CurveSpec | None`, read and write)

  The curve `(x, y, t_range)` of a point on a curve (`None` otherwise).

  Assign a new curve (every frame, for an animated one) to move the point with it: the point keeps its parameter `t` (clamped to the new range). A free or locked point cannot be given a curve.

- **`draggablePoint.coordinates`** (`Coordinates`, read and write)

  When the coordinates are shown: `"hover"`, `"always"` or `"never"`.

- **`draggablePoint.dragging`** (`bool`, read only)

  Whether the point is being dragged.

- **`draggablePoint.hovered`** (`bool`, read only)

  Whether the cursor is over the point (and it can be dragged).

- **`draggablePoint.moved`** (`bool`, read only)

  Whether the point moved between the previous frame and this one.

  Frames start at `Plane.draw_grid` (or `Plane.begin_frame`), so the value stays the same while you draw; use it to recompute something only when needed.

- **`draggablePoint.visible`** (`bool`, read only)

  Whether the point has a position that can be drawn.

- **`draggablePoint.view`** (`View`, read only)

  The view the point lives in (its plane's).

- **`draggablePoint.screen_position`** (`tuple[float, float]`, read only)

  The point's position on screen, in pixels.

- **`draggablePoint.drag_to()`**

  ```py
  draggablePoint.drag_to(px: float, py: float) -> bool
  ```

  Move the point towards a screen position, as a drag would.

  The plane calls this while the point is dragged; it can also be used to drive a point from code with screen coordinates.

  *Parameters:*

  - `px`: Screen x of the target.
  - `py`: Screen y of the target.

  *Returns:* Whether the point moved.

- **`draggablePoint.set_interaction()`**

  ```py
  draggablePoint.set_interaction(*, hovered: bool, dragging: bool)
  ```

  Record whether the point is hovered and dragged (by the plane).

  *Parameters:*

  - `hovered`: Whether the cursor is over the point.
  - `dragging`: Whether the point is being dragged.

- **`draggablePoint.begin_frame()`**

  ```py
  draggablePoint.begin_frame()
  ```

  Start a new frame: update `moved` and resample a curve when needed.

  `Plane.begin_frame` calls this for every point.

- **`draggablePoint.remove()`**

  ```py
  draggablePoint.remove()
  ```

  Remove the point from its plane: it is no longer dragged or drawn.

## Graphs

A retained list of plots, curves, points, parameters and definitions, drawn with one call each frame and saved as JSON (see the [graphs guide](graphs.md)).

### Graph

```py
pgp.Graph(
    *,
    functions: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
    view: GraphView | None = None,
)
```

An ordered list of named items: plots, curves, points, parameters, ...

Add items with `add` (one line of maths, `"y = x^2"`) or with the method for each kind (`plot`, `parametric`, `polar`, `implicit`, `point`, `points`, `polyline`, `polygon`, `draggable`, `parameter`, `define`), which take the same arguments as the plane's methods. Each returns its item, which can be changed afterwards; `graph["name"]` finds a named one.

Expressions are text in the expression language (`"a sin(x - P.x)"`, see `core.expr`) and may use the names of other items, in any order, and Python functions registered with `register` (or `functions=`). Python functions can also be given directly in place of an expression's text; such a graph can be drawn but only saved if the functions are registered.

`draw` draws the graph onto a plane; `save` and `load` (or `to_json` and `from_json`) keep it in a file.

*Parameters:*

- `functions`: Python functions that expressions can call, by name.
- `view`: What the graph is meant to be seen at (see `GraphView`).

#### Members of `Graph`

- **`graph.items`** (`tuple[Item, ...]`, read only)

  The items, in drawing order.

- **`graph.get()`**

  ```py
  graph.get(name: str, default: Item | None = None) -> Item | None
  ```

  Return the item with a name, or `default`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `name`: The name.
  - `default`: What to return if no item has it.

  *Returns:* The item, or `default`.

- **`graph.append()`**

  ```py
  graph.append(item: Item, *, index: int | None = None) -> Item
  ```

  Add an item made separately (or taken from another graph).

  *Parameters:*

  - `item`: The item.
  - `index`: Its position (default: last).

  *Returns:* The item.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If it already belongs to a graph, or its name is taken.

- **`graph.remove()`**

  ```py
  graph.remove(item: Item | str) -> Item
  ```

  Remove an item (by itself or by name).

  Its points are taken off every plane at once.

  *Parameters:*

  - `item`: The item or its name.

  *Returns:* The removed item.

  *Raises:*

  - `KeyError`: If the item is not in the graph.

- **`graph.clear()`**

  ```py
  graph.clear()
  ```

  Remove every item (registered functions and the view are kept).

- **`graph.move()`**

  ```py
  graph.move(item: Item | str, index: int)
  ```

  Move an item to another position (changing what is drawn on top).

  *Parameters:*

  - `item`: The item or its name.
  - `index`: Its new position in `items`.

  *Raises:*

  - `KeyError`: If the item is not in the graph.

- **`graph.names`** (`tuple[str, ...]`, read only)

  The names of the named items, in order.

- **`graph.functions`** (`Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]]`, read only)

  The registered Python functions, by name (see `register`).

- **`graph.register()`**

  ```py
  graph.register(name: str, func: Callable[..., Any])
  ```

  Let expressions call a Python function by name.

  The function takes NumPy arrays (or numbers) like any function given to a plane. A saved graph records the name only, so loading it needs the function again (`Graph.load(path, functions={...})`).

  *Parameters:*

  - `name`: The name expressions use.
  - `func`: The function.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If the name is invalid, or taken by an item.
  - `TypeError`: If `func` is not callable.

- **`graph.unregister()`**

  ```py
  graph.unregister(name: str)
  ```

  Forget a registered Python function.

  *Parameters:*

  - `name`: Its name.

  *Raises:*

  - `KeyError`: If no function is registered under it.

- **`graph.add()`**

  ```py
  graph.add(text: str, **options: Any) -> Item
  ```

  Add an item from one line of maths, as a graphing calculator reads it.

  ==============================  ====================================== Line                            Item ==============================  ====================================== `y = x^2` or `x^2`          a plot `f(x) = x^2`                  a plot named `f` `r = 1 + cos(θ)`              a polar curve `(cos(t), sin(t))`            a parametric curve (it uses `t`) `C = (cos(t), sin(t))`        a parametric curve named `C` `(1, 2)` or `P = (a, 2a)`   a point (named `P`) `a = 2`                       a parameter `g(u, v) = u v`               a definition `x^2 + y^2 = 9`, `x = 3`    an implicit curve (other equations) ==============================  ======================================

  *Parameters:*

  - `text`: The line.
  - `**options`: Further arguments for the item, as for the method that creates it: styles (`color="red"`), `t_range`, `domain`, `name`, ... A point with `draggable=True` becomes a draggable point (its coordinates must then be numbers), which also accepts `lock`, `curve`, and so on.

  *Returns:* The new item.

  *Raises:*

  - `ExpressionError`: If the line is not valid.
  - `GraphError`: If the name is taken.

- **`graph.plot()`**

  ```py
  graph.plot(
      expression: Expression,
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      domain: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: SamplingConfig | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PlotItem
  ```

  Add the graph of a function, `y = f(x)` (see `PlotItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.parametric()`**

  ```py
  graph.parametric(
      x: Expression | float,
      y: Expression | float,
      t_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 6.283185307179586),
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: CurveSampling | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> ParametricItem
  ```

  Add a parametric curve `(x(t), y(t))` (see `ParametricItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.polar()`**

  ```py
  graph.polar(
      r: Expression | float,
      theta_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 6.283185307179586),
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: CurveSampling | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PolarItem
  ```

  Add a polar curve `r = r(θ)` (see `PolarItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.implicit()`**

  ```py
  graph.implicit(
      expression: Expression,
      level: float | Sequence[float] = 0.0,
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      sampling: ImplicitSampling | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> ImplicitItem
  ```

  Add an implicit curve `F(x, y) = level` (see `ImplicitItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.point()`**

  ```py
  graph.point(
      position: tuple[Coordinate, Coordinate],
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      radius: float | None = None,
      marker: Any = None,
      edge_color: Any = None,
      edge_width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: PointStyle | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PointItem
  ```

  Add a point whose coordinates may be expressions (see `PointItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.points()`**

  ```py
  graph.points(
      points: Any,
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      radius: float | None = None,
      marker: Any = None,
      edge_color: Any = None,
      edge_width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: PointStyle | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PointsItem
  ```

  Add several points (see `PointsItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.polyline()`**

  ```py
  graph.polyline(
      points: Any,
      *,
      closed: bool = False,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      style: LineStyle | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PolylineItem
  ```

  Add vertices joined by straight lines (see `PolylineItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.polygon()`**

  ```py
  graph.polygon(
      points: Any,
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      color: Any = None,
      width: float | None = None,
      opacity: float | None = None,
      fill: bool | None = None,
      fill_color: Any = None,
      fill_opacity: float | None = None,
      fill_rule: Any = None,
      style: PolygonStyle | None = None,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> PolygonItem
  ```

  Add a filled polygon (see `PolygonItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.draggable()`**

  ```py
  graph.draggable(
      position: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
      *,
      name: str | None = None,
      lock: Any = None,
      curve: CurveTarget | None = None,
      t: float | None = None,
      x_range: Any = None,
      y_range: Any = None,
      color: Any = None,
      style: PointStyle | None = None,
      coordinates: Any = 'hover',
      enabled: bool = True,
      visible: bool = True,
  ) -> DraggableItem
  ```

  Add a point the user can drag (see `DraggableItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.parameter()`**

  ```py
  graph.parameter(name: str, value: Coordinate) -> ParameterItem
  ```

  Add a named value (see `ParameterItem`).

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.define()`**

  ```py
  graph.define(signature: str, expression: str) -> DefinitionItem
  ```

  Add a function for other items, not drawn (see `DefinitionItem`).

  *Parameters:*

  - `signature`: Its name and parameters, as in `"g(u, v)"`.
  - `expression`: Its value, in the parameters.

  *Returns:* The new item.

- **`graph.evaluate()`**

  ```py
  graph.evaluate(expression: str, **variables: Any) -> Any
  ```

  Evaluate an expression with the graph's names.

  For example `graph.evaluate("f(2) + a")`, or with variables, `graph.evaluate("f(x)", x=np.linspace(0, 1, 5))`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `expression`: The expression.
  - `**variables`: Values for its variables (numbers or arrays).

  *Returns:* The value: a float for numbers, an array for arrays.

  *Raises:*

  - `ExpressionError`: If the expression is not valid, or uses a name that is not defined (or has an error).

- **`graph.function()`**

  ```py
  graph.function(name: str) -> Callable[..., Any]
  ```

  Return a named function (a plot, polar or implicit curve, a definition).

  The function works on numbers and arrays, like any function of the graph, and can be plotted or differentiated directly.

  *Parameters:*

  - `name`: Its name.

  *Returns:* The function.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If no function has the name, or it has an error.

- **`graph.errors`** (`dict[Item, str]`, read only)

  The items that cannot be drawn, in order, with the reason for each.

  Errors in expressions (an unknown name, a circular definition, ...) are found without drawing; the rare errors found only when drawing (an invalid setting for a plane) are those of the last `draw`.

- **`graph.capture_view()`**

  ```py
  graph.capture_view(plane: Plane) -> GraphView
  ```

  Remember what a plane shows as the graph's `view` (saved with it).

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane.

  *Returns:* The view.

- **`graph.apply_view()`**

  ```py
  graph.apply_view(plane: Plane)
  ```

  Show the graph's `view` on a plane (nothing if it has none).

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane.

- **`graph.draw()`**

  ```py
  graph.draw(plane: Plane, surface: pygame.Surface)
  ```

  Draw every visible item onto a plane, in order, draggable points on top.

  Call it every frame, after `Plane.draw_grid`. Items with an error are skipped (see `errors`), with a `GraphWarning` the first time each error appears.

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane to draw on.
  - `surface`: The surface (usually the display).

- **`graph.detach()`**

  ```py
  graph.detach(plane: Plane)
  ```

  Take the graph's draggable points off a plane it will no longer draw on.

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane.

- **`graph.to_dict()`**

  ```py
  graph.to_dict() -> dict[str, Any]
  ```

  Return the graph as plain data (dicts, lists, strings, numbers).

  *Returns:* The data, ready for `json.dumps`.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If an item uses a Python function that is not registered (see `register`).

- **`graph.to_json()`**

  ```py
  graph.to_json(*, indent: int | None = 2) -> str
  ```

  Return the graph as JSON text (see `to_dict`).

  *Parameters:*

  - `indent`: Indentation (`None` for one line).

  *Returns:* The JSON text.

- **`graph.save()`**

  ```py
  graph.save(path: str | PathLike[str])
  ```

  Save the graph to a JSON file (UTF-8).

  *Parameters:*

  - `path`: The file.

- **`graph.from_dict()`**

  ```py
  graph.from_dict(
      data: Mapping[str, Any],
      *,
      functions: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
  ) -> Graph
  ```

  Make a graph from data made by `to_dict`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `data`: The data.
  - `functions`: The Python functions the graph was saved with.

  *Returns:* The graph.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If the data is not a valid saved graph, or needs functions that are not given.

- **`graph.from_json()`**

  ```py
  graph.from_json(
      text: str,
      *,
      functions: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
  ) -> Graph
  ```

  Make a graph from JSON text made by `to_json`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `text`: The JSON text.
  - `functions`: The Python functions the graph was saved with.

  *Returns:* The graph.

  *Raises:*

  - `GraphError`: If the text is not a valid saved graph.

- **`graph.load()`**

  ```py
  graph.load(
      path: str | PathLike[str],
      *,
      functions: Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]] | None = None,
  ) -> Graph
  ```

  Load a graph saved with `save`.

  *Parameters:*

  - `path`: The file.
  - `functions`: The Python functions the graph was saved with.

  *Raises:*

  - `OSError`: If the file cannot be read.

### GraphView

```py
pgp.GraphView(
    x_range: tuple[float, float],
    y_range: tuple[float, float],
    log_x: bool = False,
    log_y: bool = False,
    equal_aspect: bool | None = None,
)
```

A view to show a graph at, saved with it.

Ranges rather than a centre and scale are kept, so a graph opened in a window of another size shows the same part of the plane.

*Attributes:*

- `x_range`: `(x_min, x_max)`.
- `y_range`: `(y_min, y_max)`.
- `log_x`: Whether the x axis is logarithmic.
- `log_y`: Whether the y axis is logarithmic.
- `equal_aspect`: Whether both axes keep the same scale (`None` to leave the plane's setting alone). With equal aspect, the plane shows at least both ranges.

#### Members of `GraphView`

- **`graphView.of()`**

  ```py
  graphView.of(plane: Plane) -> GraphView
  ```

  Return what a plane shows now.

  Applying the result to a plane of the same size gives exactly this view again (see `View.fitted_ranges`).

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane.

  *Returns:* Its visible ranges and kinds of axes.

- **`graphView.apply()`**

  ```py
  graphView.apply(plane: Plane)
  ```

  Make a plane show this view.

  *Parameters:*

  - `plane`: The plane.

### GraphError

An invalid operation on a graph, or an invalid saved graph.

Raised for a name used twice, an item that is not in the graph, a graph that cannot be saved (an item uses a Python function that was not registered by name), or a file that is not a valid saved graph. Errors in saved graphs say where the problem is, as in `items[2].style.width: expected a number`.

### GraphWarning

An item cannot be drawn: an unknown name, a circular definition, ...

Graphs keep drawing the items that work, as a graphing calculator does, and record the problem in the item's `Item.error`. This warning is issued once each time an item's error changes, so that mistakes do not go unnoticed. Silence it with `warnings` if the errors are shown some other way (in an expression list, say).

## Graph items

The rows of a graph, made by its methods (`graph.plot(...)` returns a `PlotItem`) and changed through their attributes. They are importable from `pygridplot.graph`.

### graph.PlotItem

```py
pgp.graph.PlotItem(
    expression: Expression,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    domain: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    color: Any = None,
    width: float | None = None,
    opacity: float | None = None,
    style: LineStyle | None = None,
    sampling: SamplingConfig | None = None,
    visible: bool = True,
    palette: int | None = None,
)
```

The graph of a function, `y = f(x)`, drawn like `Plane.plot`.

A named plot also defines the function, so other items can call it: after `graph.plot("x^2", name="f")`, `"f(x - 1)"` and `"f'(x)"` work anywhere.

*Parameters:*

- `expression`: `f` as text in `x` (`"a sin(x)"`) or a function.
- `name`: The function's name (optional).
- `domain`: Draw only for `x` in `(start, end)`.
- `color`: Line colour (default: the item's palette colour).
- `width`: Line width in pixels.
- `opacity`: Line opacity.
- `style`: A `LineStyle`; the other arguments override its fields.
- `sampling`: How the function is sampled (see `SamplingConfig`); default: the plane's.
- `visible`: Whether it is drawn.
- `palette`: Palette slot (normally chosen by the graph).

#### Members of `PlotItem`

- **`plotItem.expression`** (`Expression`, read and write)

  `f`: the text in `x`, or the Python function.

- **`plotItem.domain`** (`tuple[float, float] | None`, read and write)

  The `x` interval drawn (`None` for everywhere).

- **`plotItem.sampling`** (`SamplingConfig | None`, read and write)

  Sampling settings (`None` for the plane's).

Also has the members of [`LineItem`](#graphlineitem), [`StyledItem`](#graphstyleditem), [`Item`](#graphitem).

### graph.ParametricItem

```py
pgp.graph.ParametricItem(
    x: Expression | float,
    y: Expression | float,
    t_range: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 6.283185307179586),
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    color: Any = None,
    width: float | None = None,
    opacity: float | None = None,
    style: LineStyle | None = None,
    sampling: CurveSampling | None = None,
    visible: bool = True,
    palette: int | None = None,
)
```

A parametric curve `(x(t), y(t))`, drawn like `Plane.parametric`.

A named curve can be followed by a draggable point (`graph.draggable(curve="C")`).

*Parameters:*

- `x`: `x(t)`: text in `t`, a function or a number.
- `y`: `y(t)`: likewise.
- `t_range`: `(t_min, t_max)`; one full turn by default.
- `name`: The curve's name (optional).
- `color`: Line colour (default: the item's palette colour).
- `width`: Line width in pixels.
- `opacity`: Line opacity.
- `style`: A `LineStyle`.
- `sampling`: How the curve is sampled (see `CurveSampling`).
- `visible`: Whether it is drawn.
- `palette`: Palette slot (normally chosen by the graph).

#### Members of `ParametricItem`

- **`parametricItem.x`** (`Expression | float`, read and write)

  `x(t)`: text, a function or a number.

- **`parametricItem.y`** (`Expression | float`, read and write)

  `y(t)`: text, a function or a number.

- **`parametricItem.t_range`** (`tuple[float, float]`, read and write)

  `(t_min, t_max)`.

- **`parametricItem.sampling`** (`CurveSampling | None`, read and write)

  Sampling settings (`None` for the defaults).

Also has the members of [`LineItem`](#graphlineitem), [`StyledItem`](#graphstyleditem), [`Item`](#graphitem).

### graph.DraggableItem

```py
pgp.graph.DraggableItem(
    position: tuple[float, float] | None = None,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    lock: Lock | None = None,
    curve: CurveTarget | None = None,
    t: float | None = None,
    x_range: Range | None = None,
    y_range: Range | None = None,
    color: Any = None,
    style: PointStyle | None = None,
    coordinates: Coordinates = 'hover',
    enabled: bool = True,
    visible: bool = True,
    palette: int | None = None,
)
```

A point the user drags with the mouse, like `Plane.draggable`.

The item holds the point's position, which dragging changes, setting `position` changes, and saving keeps. Other items use it as `P.x` and `P.y` (and follow it as it moves). The point can be free, locked to an axis, or kept on a curve: another item's curve (a plot, a parametric or a polar curve, by name) or one given here as `(x(t), y(t), t_range)`.

*Parameters:*

- `position`: Where it starts (needed unless it follows a curve).
- `name`: The point's name (optional).
- `lock`: `"x"` keeps x fixed, `"y"` keeps y fixed.
- `curve`: A curve item's name, or `(x(t), y(t), t_range)`.
- `t`: Starting parameter on the curve.
- `x_range`: Bounds for x (free and locked points).
- `y_range`: Bounds for y (free and locked points).
- `color`: Fill colour (default: the item's palette colour).
- `style`: A `PointStyle` (default: the plane's style for draggable points).
- `coordinates`: Show the coordinates `"hover"`, `"always"` or `"never"`.
- `enabled`: Whether it can be dragged.
- `visible`: Whether it is drawn (a hidden point cannot be dragged).
- `palette`: Palette slot (normally chosen by the graph).

#### Members of `DraggableItem`

- **`draggableItem.position`** (`tuple[float, float] | None`, read and write)

  The current position (`None` before a curve point is first drawn).

  Setting it moves the point; a point on a curve goes to the nearest point of the curve when next drawn.

- **`draggableItem.x`** (`float`, read only)

  The current x (NaN before a curve point is first drawn).

- **`draggableItem.y`** (`float`, read only)

  The current y (NaN before a curve point is first drawn).

- **`draggableItem.t`** (`float | None`, read and write)

  The parameter on the curve (`None` for free and locked points).

  Setting it moves a curve point along its curve when next drawn.

- **`draggableItem.dragging`** (`bool`, read only)

  Whether the point is being dragged on any plane.

- **`draggableItem.lock`** (`Lock | None`, read and write)

  `"x"` or `"y"` for a locked point, `None` otherwise.

- **`draggableItem.curve`** (`CurveTarget | None`, read and write)

  The curve the point follows: a curve item's name, or `(x, y, t_range)`.

- **`draggableItem.x_range`** (`Range | None`, read and write)

  Bounds for x, if any.

- **`draggableItem.y_range`** (`Range | None`, read and write)

  Bounds for y, if any.

- **`draggableItem.coordinates`** (`Coordinates`, read and write)

  When the coordinates are shown: `"hover"`, `"always"` or `"never"`.

- **`draggableItem.enabled`** (`bool`, read and write)

  Whether the point can be dragged.

- **`draggableItem.references()`**

  ```py
  draggableItem.references() -> set[str]
  ```

  Return the names of other items this point refers to (its curve's).

Also has the members of [`PointLikeItem`](#graphpointlikeitem), [`StyledItem`](#graphstyleditem), [`Item`](#graphitem).

A named value that other items use: `a = 2`.

The value is a number, or an expression of other names (`"2 b"`). Change it at any time (`graph["a"].value = 3`): everything using it follows. A number can be changed every frame without recompiling.

*Parameters:*

#### Members of `ParameterItem`

- **`parameterItem.name`** (`str`, read and write)

  The parameter's name.

  The value as given: a number or an expression.

Also has the members of [`Item`](#graphitem).


A function defined for other items, not drawn: `g(u, v) = u v + 1`.

*Parameters:*

- `name`: The function's name.
- `parameters`: The names of its arguments.
- `expression`: Its value, as text in the parameters.

#### Members of `DefinitionItem`

- **`definitionItem.name`** (`str`, read and write)

  The function's name.

- **`definitionItem.parameters`** (`tuple[str, ...]`, read and write)

Also has the members of [`Item`](#graphitem).

### graph.Item

```py
pgp.graph.Item(*, name: str | None = None, visible: bool = True)
```

A row of a graph: something drawn, or a name defined for other rows.

Subclasses describe themselves to the graph through four hooks: `_formulas()` (their formulas, with the variables of each), `_runtime(make)` (compile them with the graph's `make` into what drawing needs), `_binding(runtime)` (what their name stands for in expressions, if anything) and `_describe()` (for `repr`). Setters that change names or expressions call `_changed()`.

*Attributes:*

- `kind`: The kind of item, as written in saved graphs (`"plot"`, ...).

#### Members of `Item`

- **`item.name`** (`str | None`, read and write)

  The item's name, by which other items refer to it (`None` if unnamed).

  Renaming updates the graph; references in other items are not rewritten (they then refer to the old name, and show an error).

- **`item.visible`** (`bool`, read and write)

  Whether the item is drawn (hidden items still define their name).

- **`item.error`** (`str | None`, read only)

  Why the item cannot be drawn, or `None` if it can.

  For example `"unknown name 'b'"` or `"circular definition: f → g → f"`. Errors in expressions are always up to date (reading this checks the graph's names if anything changed); the rare errors found only when drawing are those of the last `Graph.draw`.

- **`item.graph`** (`Graph | None`, read only)

  The graph the item belongs to (`None` once removed).

- **`item.references()`**

  ```py
  item.references() -> set[str]
  ```

  Return the names of other items this item refers to.

  *Returns:* The names used in its expressions (and a followed curve), besides variables and built-ins.
